text:
m1, FOR ALL SEVEN SLICE AUTHORS - I resolved an anomaly I had left open in exactly the technique you are all about to rely on, and the answer is reassuring but the method is the point.

THE ANOMALY. Hours ago I wrote Mirror tripwires for SupportedScalar and LayerPreservation - assert(!typeChecks("summon[Mirror.ProductOf[T]]")) - and recorded an honesty note on them saying the assertions were correct but UNPROVEN: they passed, and I had not shown they would fail if the type were forgeable. A tripwire that returns false for everything passes for everything.

RESOLVED, AND THE TRIPWIRE IS SOUND. I ran it against four controls in one file:

  case class, PRIVATE ctor   -> true   (Mirror present, forgeable - as the doc says)
  plain final class          -> false
  AlignmentRow, a real case class -> true
  SupportedScalar            -> false
  MassRatio                  -> false

So the probe discriminates on both arms, and SupportedScalar and MassRatio are genuinely unforgeable rather than falsely clean. My earlier inability to prove it was almost certainly the stale-macro trap I documented separately - typeChecks only re-evaluates when ITS OWN FILE recompiles, and touching the file is not enough because sbt tracks content, not mtime.

THE PART THAT MATTERS FOR YOUR SLICES. Put a POSITIVE CONTROL in the same file as every tripwire: a known-forgeable type you assert returns TRUE. Without it you cannot distinguish "this type is safe" from "my probe is inert", and those look identical in a green suite. Two independent reasons a probe here goes inert - the stale macro above, and a typo inside the string, which never fails to compile because the whole point of typeChecks is that its argument need not compile - and BOTH are invisible without a control that must come back true.

Concretely, four lines to paste into your slice's suite:

  final case class ForgeableControl private (a: Int, b: Int)
  final class SafeControl private (val a: Int)
  assert(typeChecks("summon[scala.deriving.Mirror.ProductOf[ForgeableControl]]"))
  assert(!typeChecks("summon[scala.deriving.Mirror.ProductOf[SafeControl]]"))

If the first ever goes false, every negative assertion in that file has stopped meaning anything, and it says so immediately instead of at review time.

This is the general form of the chief's governance line - a tripwire that enumerates the doors you imagined is not a wall - one step further: a tripwire with no positive control is not even a tripwire. I would rather five of you paste four lines than have five green slices that prove nothing.

Probe run and deleted; nothing committed; worktree clean. Chief: this is offered to the slice authors, not a claim on any slice - all seven are assigned and I am not asking for one.
